Short answer: taste is subjective. People wear what they like. I may disagree with what someone else likes, but neither of us are "correct". Our tastes are our own. Long answer: Clothing is a very, very old human invention. We've literally always had it. So clothes have had a long time to be integrated into a ton of cultural traditions. As such, we all wear clothes. They're necessary for modern life. And we all understand basic rules of how to use them, some with more nuance or style than others. But none of that is really quite true about watches. Sure there is etiquette and history around what kind of watch is appropriate for which settings. But the key is, not everyone wears a watch, and extremely few of the people who do actually *need* to (as opposed to choose to.) So there is just way less cultural attention and definition over their usage. I think there's also a general generational shift away from putting much importance on clothes as a cultural signifier, but that's a whole other topic. Anyways, all of which to say, watches never really developed an "objective" (depending on who you ask) correct size. As in all things, watch design is subject to fashions and trends, but in clothing, there are actual rules (in addition to fashion and trends too, of course)

Tastes evolve, and people change. There's no reason to think you five years from now will like exactly the same thing as you today. Now if you're talking a shirt or cheaper article of clothing, we mostly accept that once purchased, that money is gone, and the item's resale value is negligible. But if you're talking about a high-end watch, that's a much different proposition, especially because the watch in question does not, personally, to me, have what i would call a timeless design, making it more likely to be something you may not care for down the road.  Now, f you're a person who doesn't care about watches and buy one just to have it and not think about, and you're confident one watch will last you your entire life, then resale value isn't important. But unless you're a professional or someone for whom this amount of money is literally not a concern, then this type of person probably doesn't buy a high-end watch.  Last, if you're a collector or watch enthusiast, you probably own more than you need, and probably buy and sell watches with some regularity, in which case the option to not lose a bunch of money just because your tastes have evolved is a nice option.  So the bottom line is that while resale value is not important to all people in all circumstances, it's important to enough people in enough circumstances that I personally would factor it into my buying decision.
